title: Lesson 3 Quiz: Inflation, Purchasing Power, and Living Standards
description: A short quiz to check what you learned in this lesson. Submitting it completes the lesson's quiz requirement, and your score is recorded separately.

history.note: AI-written question draft. Not reviewed or approved by a human (admin); do not give to students.

questions.prompt: Hypothetical example: A household basket in Country W cost $250 in the base year and costs $265 this year. What is this year's price index (base year = 100)? (Enter a number only.)
Hypothetical example: Country X's inflation rate fell from 6% last year to 3% this year. What happened to the price level this year?

choices.text: The price level fell, because a drop in inflation means prices went down
The price level fell by 3 percent, the size of the drop in the inflation rate
The price level stayed the same, because inflation is now below last year's rate
The price level still rose, but by about 3 percent rather than about 6 percent

questions.prompt: Hypothetical example: A worker's nominal wage rises 3% this year while the price index rises 5%. By about what percent does the worker's real wage change? Round to one decimal place and enter a negative number for a decrease. (Enter a number only, in percent.)
Hypothetical example: A bank makes a one-year loan at a fixed 4% interest rate, expecting 2% inflation. Inflation turns out to be 7%. Who gains from this surprise?

choices.text: The borrower gains, because the loan is repaid with dollars that buy less
The bank gains, because higher prices raise the value of what it is repaid
Neither side gains, because the interest rate was fixed in the contract
Both sides gain, because inflation raises everyone's income in dollars

questions.prompt: Which is the best reason that central banks generally aim for low, stable inflation rather than high or unpredictable inflation?

choices.text: Low inflation means that the prices of individual goods stop changing over time
Unpredictable inflation blurs price signals and makes saving and contracts riskier
High inflation raises the real wages of workers whose pay is set in fixed dollars
Stable inflation lets the government set most prices directly instead of markets
